cultivar: Qingxin (Qing Xin oolong, also called Ruan Zhi); Jin Xuan and Si Ji Chun lots are sometimes sold in the same style
processing: Moderately oxidised (traditionally around 25–35%, modern lots often lighter), ball-rolled in cloth over many cycles, then given a light to medium roast, traditionally over longan-wood charcoal; the roast is what separates it from the green high-mountain style.
harvest_season: Spring (April–May) and winter (late October–November) are the two main harvests and the ones entered in competitions; summer and autumn pickings exist but are cheaper and plainer.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly glossy dark-green to olive half-balls with a few short stems, darker and duller than high-mountain tea because of the roast.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden-yellow to light amber depending on the roast level.
appearance_wet: Thick whole leaves open to a dark olive green with reddish-brown edges and a soft, oily feel.
taste_profile: Toasted grain and warm buttery sweetness up front, orchid and ripe fruit underneath, with a thick, soft mouthfeel and a long, gently roasty finish.

brewing.notes: Water at or just off the boil; rolled leaf needs a slightly longer first steep to open. A clay pot flatters the roast, a porcelain gaiwan shows more of the florals.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest: the spring and winter crops of the current year, with winter Dong Ding often a little thicker and spring more fragrant. The Lugu Farmers' Association competition, held after each of those harvests, grades lots from Special (特等) through First (頭等), Second, Third and the 'plum blossom' tiers and sells them in sealed, numbered 300 g packs at a steep premium over ordinary garden tea. Roasted lots keep well for a year or two, and the heavier roasts are sometimes aged on purpose, but everyday Dong Ding is best within a year of its roast.
description:
Dong Ding is the tea most Taiwanese drinkers mean when they say 'oolong' without any qualifier: a ball-rolled Qing Xin oolong from the villages around the Dong Ding hill in Lugu Township, Nantou, at roughly 600–800 metres. It is not high-mountain tea by Taiwan's definition (that label starts at 1,000 metres); what sets it apart is that it is roasted, so it drinks warmer and rounder than the green, floral high-mountain style that came later. The story that the bushes arrived from Wuyi in the 1850s with a scholar named Lin Fengchi is a local legend, repeated on every sign in Lugu.

The leaf is withered in the sun and then indoors with repeated tossing, oxidised further than high-mountain tea, pan-fired, and rolled in cloth bundles over and over until it curls into tight half-spheres. Then comes the roast: hours or days in bamboo baskets or ovens, traditionally over longan-wood charcoal, which turns raw florals into toasted grain, honey and dried fruit and gives the liquor its gold-to-amber colour. Lightly roasted modern lots sit close to high-mountain tea; traditional lots are unmistakably toasty.

In the cup you get buttery sweetness and toasted cereal first, then orchid and a ripe fruitiness underneath, with a thick texture and a finish that stays warm in the throat. It holds up to seven or eight steeps and does not turn harsh when pushed. The common mistake is brewing it like a delicate green oolong: it wants fully boiling water and a proper dose of leaf, and a clay pot suits the roast.

It is sold by season, spring and winter, and increasingly by competition grade: the Lugu Farmers' Association runs the largest tea competition in Taiwan twice a year, and winning lots go out in sealed, numbered 300 g boxes at prices far above garden tea. 'Dong Ding' is also used loosely as a style name, so tea from Mingjian or elsewhere, and Jin Xuan or Si Ji Chun leaf, is often sold under it; ask for the cultivar and whether it was actually grown in Lugu.

If the roast is what you like, go deeper with a charcoal-roasted Dong Ding or a Hong Shui oolong; if it is the florals, Shan Lin Xi or Alishan will show you the same cultivar without the fire.
sources_note: Lugu competition grade names and the 300 g (half-jin) pack convention are from memory of the Farmers' Association system; worth checking the current tier list.
